props.title: How to Murder Your Wife

sections.content: **How to Murder Your Wife** (1965) stands as a fascinating artifact of 1960s comedy that walks a precarious tightrope between dark humor and dated gender politics. Jack Lemmon delivers a characteristically energetic performance as Stanley Ford, a successful cartoonist living the bachelor dream until Italian bombshell Virna Lisi enters his life during a drunken wedding. The film shares DNA with other marriage-skeptical comedies of its era like **The Marriage-Go-Round** (1961) and **Boeing Boeing** (1965), but pushes the premise into darker territory through Stanley's newspaper comic strip about a secret agent who plots to kill his wife.

sections.content: Director Richard Quine, who previously directed Lemmon in **Bell Book and Candle** (1958) and **It Should Happen to You** (1954), brings a glossy sophistication to the proceedings while maintaining the screwball energy required for the increasingly outlandish plot. The film's treatment of marriage as a form of imprisonment for men reflects common comedic tropes of the era, seen similarly in **A Guide for the Married Man** (1967) and **Divorce American Style** (1967), though modern viewers may find the casual misogyny harder to stomach. SUBHEAD: Cultural Context and Legacy

While **How to Murder Your Wife** plays its murderous fantasy for laughs, it exists in interesting conversation with more serious films about domestic discord from the same period, like **Diary of a Mad Housewife** (1970) and **The War Between Men and Women** (1972). The film's elaborate bachelor pad gadgetry and lifestyle porn aspects presage later works about male arrested development like **Big** (1988) and **The 40-Year-Old Virgin** (2005). Terry-Thomas provides crucial support as Harold, Stanley's devoted butler, continuing the tradition of scene-stealing servants that includes **Arthur** (1981) and **The Remains of the Day** (1993).
